[ORIGINAL TEXT]: Overview Our method consists of three parts. The core component is the rotamer density estimator (RDE),  a conditional normalizing flow that models the probability density of sidechain conformations (rotamers) given the amino acid type and environments (Section 3.2). Next is the algorithm for estimating the entropy of the distribution parameterized by the normalizing flow (Section 3.3). Finally, we show how to use the entropy of the  mutated and wild-type protein-protein interfaces at both bound and unbound states to estimate the change in binding free energy ( ∆∆ G ) upon mutation, and how to use neural networks to predict ∆∆ G more accurately using the unsupervised representations from the RDE (Section 3.4). A protein-protein complex is a multi-chain protein structure that can be divided into two groups. Each group contains at least one protein chain and each chain consists of multiple amino acids. For a protein complex containing n amino acids, we number them from 1 to n . The two groups of the complex can be represented by two disjoint sets of indices A, B ⊂ { 1 . . . n } An amino acid is characterised by its type, position, orientation, and sidechain conformation. We denote the type, position, and orientation of the i -th ( i ∈ { 1 . . . n } ) amino acid as a i ∈ { 1 . . . 20 } , p i ∈ R 3 , and O i ∈ SO (3) respectively. The sidechain conformation of the amino acid is called rotamer . As the conformational degree of freedom of the sidechain is defined by rotatable bonds, a rotamer can be sufficiently parameterized by torsional angles w.r.t. the rotatable bonds. The number of torsional angles vary between 0 to 4 depending on the amino acid type. For an amino acid with d torsional angles, we denote the k -th ( k ∈ { 1 . . . 4 } ) torsional angle by χ ( k ) i ∈ [0 , 2 π ) . Collectively, all the torsional angles are denoted by a vector χ i = ( χ ( k ) i ) dk =1 . Using the language of geometry, an angle can  represented by a point on the unit circle S 1 . A vector consisting of d angular values reside on the product of d unit circle, known as the d -dimensional torus T D = ( S 1 ) D .

Next is the algorithm for estimating the entropy of the distribution parameterized by the normalizing flow (Section 3.3). Lastly, we demonstrate how to utilize the entropy of the mutated and wild-type protein-protein interfaces at both bound and unbound states to estimate the change in binding free energy (∆∆ G) upon mutation, and how to use neural networks to predict ∆∆ G more accurately using the unsupervised representations from the RDE (Section 3.4). For a protein complex containing n residues, we label them from 1 to n. The two groups of the complex can be represented by two disjoint sets of indices A, B ⊂ {1, …, n}. A residue is characterized by its type, position, orientation, and sidechain conformation. We denote the type, position, and orientation of the i-th (i ∈ {1, …, n}) residue as a i ∈ {1, …, 20}, p i ∈ R³, and O i ∈ SO(3), respectively. The sidechain conformation of the residue is referred to as a rotamer. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Deep CNN is ﬁrstly utilized for image SR in SRCNN (Dong et al., 2014) and  continuously shows promising SR performance. There are only three convolutional (Conv) layers in SRCNN, hindering its performance. Kim et al . increased the network depth in VDSR (Kim et al., 2016a) with residual learning and obtained notable improvements over SRCNN. Lim et al . (Lim et al., 2017) built a much deeper network EDSR by using simpliﬁed residual blocks. Zhang et al . (Zhang et al., 2018b) proposed RCAN, which is one of the deepest networks in SR. With increased network size, very deep networks, like EDSR (Lim et al., 2017) and RCAN (Zhang et al., 2018b), have achieved remarkable SR performance. However, they also suffer from heavy model parameters, number of operations, and inference time. Therefore, it is  infeasible to directly deploy them on resource-limited platformswithout neural processing units or off-chip memory (Lee et al., 2020).

Kim et al. increased the network depth in VDSR (Kim et al., 2016a) with residual learning and obtained notable improvements over SRCNN. Lim et al. (Lim et al., 2017) built a much deeper network EDSR by using simpliﬁed residual blocks. Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2018b) proposed RCAN, which is one of the deepest networks in SR. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: On the other hand, neural network pruning is well-known as an effective technique to reduce model complexity (Reed, 1993; Sze et al., 2017). For acceleration, researchers mainly focus on ﬁlter pruning (a.k.a. structured pruning) (Li et al., 2017) rather than weight-element pruning (a.k.a. unstructured pruning) (Han et al., 2015; 2016b). Marrying ﬁlter pruning with image SR seems a plausible solution to strike a better performance-complexity trade-off. However,  ﬁlter pruning methods in classiﬁcation can hardly translate to  SR networks directly. The main reason is that, residual connections are well-known hard to prune in structured pruning (Li et al., 2017) while they are extensively used in state-of-the-art  SR networks (e.g., EDSR (Lim et al., 2017) has 32 residual blocks; RCAN (Zhang et al., 2018b) even has nested residual blocks).

[INSTRUCTION]: Improve the paragraph.

[ANSWER]: On the other hand, neural network pruning is well-known as an effective technique to reduce model complexity (Reed, 1993; Sze et al., 2017). For acceleration, researchers mainly focus on filter pruning (a.k.a. structured pruning) (Li et al., 2017) rather than weight-element pruning (a.k.a. unstructured pruning) (Han et al., 2015; 2016b). Integrating filter pruning with image super-resolution (SR) seems a plausible solution to achieve a better performance-complexity trade-off. However, filter pruning methods in classification can hardly be directly applied to SR networks. The primary reason is that residual connections are known to be difficult to prune in structured pruning (Li et al., 2017), while they are extensively utilized in state-of-the-art SR networks (e.g., EDSR (Lim et al., 2017) contains 32 residual blocks; RCAN (Zhang et al., 2018b) even incorporates nested residual blocks).

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: What makes OOD detection particularly challenging? To explain this, modern neural networks are commonly optimized on thein-distribution (ID) data only, and lack explicit knowledge of unknowns during training time. The resulting decision boundary, despite being useful on ID tasks such as classiﬁcation, can undesirably cover OOD data. We illustrate this in Figure 1. The ID data (gray) consists of three class-conditional Gaussians, on which a three-way softmax classiﬁer is trained. The resulting classiﬁer is overconﬁdent for regions far away from the ID data (see the red shade in Figure 1(b)). When such models are directly employed, the decision boundary can be ill-fated for OOD detection. Ideally, a model should learn a more compact decision boundary that produces low uncertainty for the ID data, with high OOD uncertainty elsewhere ( e.g. , Figure 1(c)). However, achieving this goal is non-trivial due to the lack of supervision signal of unknowns. It is hard to comprehensively anticipate unknown data in advance under a large space of OOD uncertainty. This prompts thefollowing question: How can we enable unknown-aware deep neural networks without explicit knowledge of the unknowns in advance?

[INSTRUCTION]: Rewrite this paragraph to make it more concise and convincing.

[ANSWER]: OOD detection is particularly challenging because modern neural networks are generally optimized on in-distribution (ID) data alone, lacking knowledge of unknowns during training. Consequently, the resulting decision boundary, although effective for ID tasks like classification, can inadvertently include OOD data. Figure 1 illustrates this issue: the ID data (gray) comprises three class-conditional Gaussians, and a three-way softmax classifier trained on it becomes overconfident in regions distant from the ID data, as seen by the red shade in Figure 1(b). Directly using such models yields an inadequate decision boundary for OOD detection. An ideal model would have a compact decision boundary with low ID uncertainty and high OOD uncertainty elsewhere (e.g., Figure 1(c)), but achieving this is difficult without a supervision signal for unknowns. Predicting unknown data in advance across a broad OOD uncertainty space is challenging, leading to the question: How can we develop unknown-aware deep neural networks without pre-existing knowledge of the unknowns?

Further, due to the intrinsic difference between categorical and continuous label space, the common intuitions for classiﬁcation, e.g. cluster assumptions or pseudo labeling strategies, cannot be naturally adapted into deep regression. To this end, we ﬁrst delved into the existing data-efﬁcient methods in deep learning and found that they either encourage invariance to data stochasticity ( e.g. , consistency regularization under different augmentations) or model stochasticity ( e.g. , difference penalty for predictions of models with different dropout). To take the power of both worlds, we propose a novel χ -model by simultaneously encouraging the invariance to data stochasticity and model stochasticity. Further, the χ -model plays a minimax game between the feature extractor and task-speciﬁc heads to further enhance the invariance to model stochasticity. Extensive experiments verify the superiority of the χ -model among various tasks, from a single-value prediction task of age estimation to a dense-value prediction task of keypoint localization, a 2D synthetic and a 3D realistic dataset, as well as a multi-category object recognition task.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: A gap in the literature seems to be a practical completeness threshold for cost optimal planning problems that have actions with 0-cost. This is one hurdle to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems since, without a reasonable completeness threshold, optimality can only be proved after solving the compilation for a horizon that is the number of states in the state space. This is impractical for most problems since it can be exponentially bigger than the size of the given problem. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. Optimality of a given solution is then proved when this over-approximation is unsatisﬁable. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: A gap in the literature seems to be a practical completeness threshold for cost optimal planning problems that have actions with 0-cost. This is impractical for most problems since it can be exponentially bigger than the size of the given problem. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. [ANSWER]: A gap exists in the literature regarding a practical completeness threshold for cost-optimal planning problems that incorporate actions with a cost of zero. This is a significant hurdle to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems because, without an acceptable completeness threshold, optimality can only be proven following the resolution of the compilation for a horizon equal to the number of states in the state space. This is impractical for most problems as the size of the compilation can be exponentially larger than the given problem. It is important to note that some approaches aim to bypass the requirement for a tight completeness threshold. For instance, those proposed by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al. add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. The optimality of a given solution is then established when this over-approximation is unsatisfiable. The resulting decision boundary, despite being useful on ID tasks such as classiﬁcation, can undesirably cover OOD data. We illustrate this in Figure 1. The ID data (gray) consists of three class-conditional Gaussians, on which a three-way softmax classiﬁer is trained. The resulting classiﬁer is overconﬁdent for regions far away from the ID data (see the red shade in Figure 1(b)). When such models are directly employed, the decision boundary can be ill-fated for OOD detection. Ideally, a model should learn a more compact decision boundary that produces low uncertainty for the ID data, with high OOD uncertainty elsewhere ( e.g. , Figure 1(c)). However, achieving this goal is non-trivial due to the lack of supervision signal of unknowns. It is hard to comprehensively anticipate unknown data in advance under a large space of OOD uncertainty. [ANSWER]: Modern neural networks, optimized solely on in-distribution (ID) data, lack awareness of unknowns during training, compromising their ability to effectively distinguish ID data from out-of-distribution (OOD) data. The classifier, overconfident in regions distant from ID data (red shade, Figure 1b), can result in an ill-suited decision boundary for OOD detection. Anticipating comprehensive unknown data is complicated under vast OOD uncertainty, raising the question: How can we develop unknown-aware deep neural networks without prior knowledge of the unknowns?

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: Proactive Motion Capture Few previous works studied proactive motion capture with a single mobile camera (Zhou et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2018; Kiciroglu et al., 2019). In comparison, more works studied the control of a multi-camera team. Among them, many are based on optimization with various system designs, including marker-based (Nägeli et al., 2018), RGBD-based (Xu et al., 2017), two-stage system (Saini et al., 2019; Tallamraju et al., 2019), hierarchical system (Ho et al., 2021), etc . It is important to note that all the above methods deal with static occlusion sources or clean landscapes. Also, the common similarity shared by these works is the use of hand-crafted optimization objectives and some fixed-form camera formations. These factors resulted in poor adaptability to dynamic scenes saturated with uncertainties. Recently, RL-based methods received more attention due to their potential for dynamic formation adjustments. These works focused on active 3D HPE in the Gazebo simulation (Tallamraju et al., 2020) or Panoptic dome (Joo et al., 2015; Pirinen et al., 2019; Gärtner et al., 2020) for active view selection. Among them, AirCapRL (Tallamraju et al., 2020) shares similarities with our work. However, it is restricted to coordinating between two cameras in clean landscapes without occlusion. We study the collaboration between more cameras  and resolve the credit assignment issue with  novel CTCR incentives. Meanwhile, we consider a more challenging scenario with multiple distracting humans  as  dynamic occlusions, which requires dedicated algorithms to handle.

[ANSWER]: Few previous studies have investigated proactive motion capture using a single mobile camera (Zhou et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2018; Kiciroglu et al., 2019). In contrast, more research has focused on controlling a multi-camera team. Among these, many approaches rely on optimization with various system designs, including marker-based (Nägeli et al., 2018), RGBD-based (Xu et al., 2017), two-stage systems (Saini et al., 2019; Tallamraju et al., 2019), and hierarchical systems (Ho et al., 2021), among others. Notably, all these methods address static occlusion sources or clean landscapes. Moreover, they share a common trait: the use of hand-crafted optimization objectives and fixed-form camera formations. These factors result in poor adaptability to dynamic scenes characterized by uncertainties. Recently, reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods have gained attention due to their potential for dynamic formation adjustments. These studies have focused on active 3D human pose estimation (HPE) in the Gazebo simulation (Tallamraju et al., 2020) or Panoptic dome (Joo et al., 2015; Pirinen et al., 2019; Gärtner et al., 2020) for active view selection. Among them, AirCapRL (Tallamraju et al., 2020) shares similarities with our work. However, it is restricted to coordinating between two cameras in clean landscapes without occlusion. In contrast, we investigate the collaboration between multiple cameras and resolve the credit assignment issue with novel CTCR incentives. Furthermore, we consider a more challenging scenario with multiple distracting humans as dynamic occlusions, which requires dedicated algorithms to handle.

This is one hurdle to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems since, without a reasonable completeness threshold, optimality can only be proved after solving the compilation for a horizon that is the number of states in the state space. This is impractical for most problems since it can be exponentially bigger than the size of the given problem. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. Nonetheless, these approaches still need to compute compilations for multiple horizons and they are susceptible to having to solve compilations for an exponential horizon, unless a tighter completeness threshold is available, since the over-approximation is a relaxation of the given problem, i.e. it could be solvable even if the concrete problem is not solvable.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: To mitigate the burden of data labeling, we aim at improving data efﬁciency for both classiﬁcation and regression setups in deep learning. However, the current focus is on classiﬁcation problems while rare attention has been paid to deep regression, which usually requires more human effort to labeling. Further, due to the intrinsic difference between categorical and continuous label space, the common intuitions for classiﬁcation, e.g. cluster assumptions or pseudo labeling strategies, cannot be naturally adapted into deep regression. To this end, we ﬁrst delved into the existing data-efﬁcient methods in deep learning and found that they either encourage invariance to data stochasticity ( e.g. , consistency regularization under different augmentations) or model stochasticity ( e.g. , difference penalty for predictions of models with different dropout). To take the power of both worlds, we propose a novel χ -model by simultaneously encouraging the invariance to data stochasticity and model stochasticity. Further, the χ -model plays a minimax game between the feature extractor and task-speciﬁc heads to further enhance the invariance to model stochasticity. Extensive experiments verify the superiority of the χ -model among various tasks, from a single-value prediction task of age estimation to a dense-value prediction task of keypoint localization, a 2D synthetic and a 3D realistic dataset, as well as a multi-category object recognition task.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: What makes OOD detection particularly challenging? To explain this, modern neural networks are commonly optimized on thein-distribution (ID) data only, and lack explicit knowledge of unknowns during training time. The resulting decision boundary, despite being useful on ID tasks such as classiﬁcation, can undesirably cover OOD data. We illustrate this in Figure 1. The ID data (gray) consists of three class-conditional Gaussians, on which a three-way softmax classiﬁer is trained. The resulting classiﬁer is overconﬁdent for regions far away from the ID data (see the red shade in Figure 1(b)). When such models are directly employed, the decision boundary can be ill-fated for OOD detection. Ideally, a model should learn a more compact decision boundary that produces low uncertainty for the ID data, with high OOD uncertainty elsewhere ( e.g. , Figure 1(c)). However, achieving this goal is non-trivial due to the lack of supervision signal of unknowns. It is hard to comprehensively anticipate unknown data in advance under a large space of OOD uncertainty. This prompts thefollowing question: How can we enable unknown-aware deep neural networks without explicit knowledge of the unknowns in advance?

[ANSWER]: OOD detection is particularly challenging because modern neural networks are typically optimized solely on in-distribution (ID) data, lacking explicit knowledge of unknowns during training. This is illustrated in Figure 1, where the ID data (gray) consists of three class-conditional Gaussians used to train a three-way softmax classifier. The resulting classifier exhibits overconfidence in regions outside the ID data (see red shade in Figure 1(b)). Direct application of such models can prove detrimental for OOD detection. Ideally, a model would establish a compact decision boundary that maintains low uncertainty for ID data and high uncertainty for OOD data (e.g., Figure 1(c)). However, achieving this is challenging due to the absence of supervision signals for unknowns and the difficulty of anticipating diverse unknown data across a vast OOD uncertainty space. This raises the question: How can we enable unknown-aware deep neural networks without prior explicit knowledge of the unknowns?

A protein-protein complex is a multi-chain protein structure that can be divided into two groups. Each group contains at least one protein chain and each chain consists of multiple amino acids. For a protein complex containing n amino acids, we number them from 1 to n . Collectively, all the torsional angles are denoted by a vector χ i = ( χ ( k ) i ) dk =1 . Using the language of geometry, an angle can  represented by a point on the unit circle S 1 . [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, they are impractical or neglected to be extended to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, like neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically consume considerable computation resources. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. Nevertheless, it is challenging to apply directly to SR networks, as filter pruning for residual blocks is notoriously tricky. To address these issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to ensure that the locations of pruned filters are aligned across different layers. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, they are impractical or neglected to be extended to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, like neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically consume considerable computation resources. In contrast, network pruning is a cheap and effective model compression technique. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. [ANSWER]: Temporal logic (TL)-guided policy learning is an area that has inspired our work. Unlike these methods, our method, STL, operates on continuous signals, allowing us to learn from continuous demonstration trajectories, which are more readily available in robotic systems. Our proposed LogicRiskNet is also learnable from demonstrations.

Statistical methods are based on feature engineering. Descriptors that summarize the geometric, physical, evolutionary, and motif properties of proteinsare used to fit the statistical model that predicts the effect of mutations on binding free energy (Geng et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2020). Traditional methodsgenerally face the trade-off between speed and accuracy due to the time-consuming sampling process. Sophisticated energy functions and feature engineering underlying these methods depend heavily on human knowledge, thus limiting their pace to improve with the fast-growing of available protein structures.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: A gap in the literature seems to be a practical completeness threshold for cost optimal planning problems that have actions with 0-cost. This is one hurdle to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems since, without a reasonable completeness threshold, optimality can only be proved after solving the compilation for a horizon that is the number of states in the state space. This is impractical for most problems since it can be exponentially bigger than the size of the given problem. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. Optimality of a given solution is then proved when this over-approximation is unsatisﬁable. Nonetheless, these approaches still need to compute compilations for multiple horizons and they are susceptible to having to solve compilations for an exponential horizon, unless a tighter completeness threshold is available, since the over-approximation is a relaxation of the given problem, i.e. it could be solvable even if the concrete problem is not solvable.

[INSTRUCTION]: Improve the English of this paragraph.

[ANSWER]: A noticeable lacuna in the existing literature appears to be a practical completeness threshold for cost-optimal planning problems featuring actions with zero cost. This represents a significant barrier to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems, as the optimality of a solution can only be guaranteed after solving the compilation for a horizon equivalent to the size of the state space, which can be exponentially larger than the original problem size. Notably, some approaches attempt to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, as exemplified by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., who incorporate an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem into the encoding. Optimality is then established when this over-approximation is found to be unsatisfiable. Nevertheless, these methods still require the computation of compilations for multiple horizons and are susceptible to having to solve compilations for an exponential horizon, unless a tighter completeness threshold is available, since the over-approximation is a relaxation of the original problem, implying that it may be solvable even if the concrete problem is not.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, they are impractical or neglected to be extended to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, like neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically consume considerable computation resources. In contrast, network pruning is a cheap and effective model compression technique. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. We conduct extensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger image SR networks. SRPN-L and SRPN achieve superior performance gains over recent methods quantitatively and visually.

In contrast, network pruning is an economical and effective method for model compression. However, its application to SR networks presents challenges, especially with respect to the pruning of filters in residual blocks. To tackle these challenges, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to maintain the alignment of pruned filters across different layers. Extensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger image SR networks have been executed, yielding superior performance gains for SRPN-L and SRPN, both quantitatively and visually.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: Training ﬂow-based encoders The next challenge is to design a training procedure for our newly proposed architecture. The main issue is that the statistical distance is not differentiable (as classiﬁer µ ∗ is binary) so wewant to replace it with a differentiable proxy. Pinsker’s inequality guarantees that the statistical distance between Zand Z 1 can be bounded using symmetrized KL divergence between Z 0 and Z 1 (see Appendix A. for more detailed proof). We show a high-level description of our training procedure in Algorithm 1. In each step, we sample a batch of x 0 and xfrom the respective distributions and encode them to the representations z 0 and z 1 . We then estimate a symmetrized KL-divergence between distributions Z 0 and Z 1 , denoted as L 0 + L 1 , and combine it with a classiﬁcation loss L clf using tradeoff parameter γ , and run a gradient step to minimize the joint loss. While we use a convex scalarization scheme to obtain the joint loss in Algorithm 1, our approach is independent of the concrete multi-objective optimization objective. We will demonstrate the compatibility with other scalarization schemes in Appendix C.

We combine this with a classification loss L clf using a tradeoff parameter γ and minimize the joint loss through gradient descent. Our approach is independent of the optimization objective's scalarization scheme.

[ANSWER]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have demonstrated promising results with moderate model sizes. Nevertheless, extending these approaches to larger networks often proves impractical or is overlooked. Concurrently, model compression techniques, such as neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically require substantial computational resources. In contrast, network pruning emerges as a cost-effective and efficient model compression technique. However, its application to SR networks is challenging, particularly due to the complexities associated with filter pruning in residual blocks. To tackle these challenges, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SPRP), which implements regularization on the pruned structure to ensure that the locations of pruned filters remain consistent across different layers. Specifically, for layers interconnected by the same residual, we identify filters with identical indices as unimportant. To transfer the expressive power of the unimportant filters to the remaining network components, we utilize L2 regularization to drive the weights of these filters towards zero, thereby ensuring that their removal will result in minimal performance degradation. We apply SPRP to train efficient image SR networks, culminating in the development of a lightweight network known as SPRN-L and a notably deep network, SPRN. Our extensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger image SR networks indicate that SPRN-L and SPRN achieve superior performance gains over recent methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: A gap in the literature seems to be a practical completeness threshold for cost optimal planning problems that have actions with 0-cost. This is one hurdle to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems since, without a reasonable completeness threshold, optimality can only be proved after solving the compilation for a horizon that is the number of states in the state space. This is impractical for most problems since it can be exponentially bigger than the size of the given problem. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. Optimality of a given solution is then proved when this over-approximation is unsatisﬁable. Nonetheless, these approaches still need to compute compilations for multiple horizons and they are susceptible to having to solve compilations for an exponential horizon, unless a tighter completeness threshold is available, since the over-approximation is a relaxation of the given problem, i.e. it could be solvable even if the concrete problem is not solvable.

Further, due to the intrinsic difference between categorical and continuous label space, the common intuitions for classiﬁcation, e.g. cluster assumptions or pseudo labeling strategies, cannot be naturally adapted into deep regression. To this end, we ﬁrst delved into the existing data-efﬁcient methods in deep learning and found that they either encourage invariance to data stochasticity ( e.g. , consistency regularization under different augmentations) or model stochasticity ( e.g. , difference penalty for predictions of models with different dropout). Further, the χ -model plays a minimax game between the feature extractor and task-speciﬁc heads to further enhance the invariance to model stochasticity. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: A gap in the literature seems to be a practical completeness threshold for cost optimal planning problems that have actions with 0-cost. This is one hurdle to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems since, without a reasonable completeness threshold, optimality can only be proved after solving the compilation for a horizon that is the number of states in the state space. This is impractical for most problems since it can be exponentially bigger than the size of the given problem. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. Optimality of a given solution is then proved when this over-approximation is unsatisﬁable. Nonetheless, these approaches still need to compute compilations for multiple horizons and they are susceptible to having to solve compilations for an exponential horizon, unless a tighter completeness threshold is available, since the over-approximation is a relaxation of the given problem, i.e. it could be solvable even if the concrete problem is not solvable.

[ANSWER]: A notable gap in the literature appears to be the lack of a practical completeness threshold for cost-optimal planning problems featuring actions with 0-cost. This poses a significant hurdle to the application of SAT-based planning to such problems, as without a reasonable completeness threshold, optimality can only be proven after solving the compilation for a horizon equal to the number of states in the state space. This approach is impractical for most problems, as the horizon can be exponentially larger than the size of the given problem. It is worth noting that some approaches attempt to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such as those proposed by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which incorporate an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem into the encoding. Optimality of a given solution is then proven when this over-approximation is unsatisfiable. Nonetheless, these approaches still require computing compilations for multiple horizons and are susceptible to having to solve compilations for an exponential horizon, unless a tighter completeness threshold is available, since the over-approximation is a relaxation of the given problem, i.e., it may be solvable even if the concrete problem is not solvable.

Among them, AirCapRL (Tallamraju et al., 2020) shares similarities with our work. However, it is restricted to coordinating between two cameras in clean landscapes without occlusion. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Temporal logic (TL)-guided policy learning is an area that we take have taken inspiration from. In this area, TL is often used to specify the ego agent’s desired high-level behavior and used to generaterewards. The authors of [17, 18, 19] provide surveys of recent work on the use of TL in RL. The exploration problem still exists in these methods. The authors of [20, 21] learns ﬁnite state automata from demonstration and use them to guide planning with the value iteration network which avoids exploration. It can sometimes be tedious to manually design a TL formula that yields satisfying behaviors. Work has been done to make components of the formula learnable from data. In [22]learns linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas from demonstrations. Given the close relationship between TL and automaton[23], the authors of [24] proposes a method that learns reward machines (an automata-like reward presentation) from demonstrations. A commonality to these methods is that the LTL that they use operate on propositions (binary variables with values true or false). Therefore,either high-level demonstrations (proposition traces) or a mapping from low-level states to propositions is required. This also limits these methods to operate on discreteand ﬁnite state and actionspaces. Our method works with STL which operates on continuous signals, therefore, we are able tolearn from continuous demonstration trajectories which is more readily available in robotic systems. The LogicRiskNet that we propose is also learnable from demonstrations.

[ANSWER]: Temporal logic (TL), which is used to guide policy learning by specifying ego agents' desired behavior and generating rewards, has inspired our work. These methods face the exploration problem, addressed in [20, 21] through learning finite state automata from demonstrations and planning with a value iteration network. Though manually designing TL formulas can be tedious, methods such as [22] learn LTL formulas from demonstrations and [24] propose learning reward machines from demonstrations. While these approaches rely on propositions, our approach using signal temporal logic (STL) allows us to learn from continuous demonstration trajectories, providing more readily available data in robotic systems. Our proposed LogicRiskNet is also learnable from demonstrations.

Among them, AirCapRL (Tallamraju et al., 2020) shares similarities with our work. However, it is restricted to coordinating between two cameras in clean landscapes without occlusion. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, they are impractical or neglected to be extended to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, like neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically consume considerable computation resources. In contrast, network pruning is a cheap and effective model compression technique. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. We conduct extensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger image SR networks. SRPN-L and SRPN achieve superior performance gains over recent methods quantitatively and visually.

Further, due to the intrinsic difference between categorical and continuous label space, the common intuitions for classiﬁcation, e.g. cluster assumptions or pseudo labeling strategies, cannot be naturally adapted into deep regression. Further, the χ -model plays a minimax game between the feature extractor and task-speciﬁc heads to further enhance the invariance to model stochasticity. Further, due to the intrinsic difference between categorical and continuous label space, the common intuitions for classiﬁcation, e.g. cluster assumptions or pseudo labeling strategies, cannot be naturally adapted into deep regression. To this end, we ﬁrst delved into the existing data-efﬁcient methods in deep learning and found that they either encourage invariance to data stochasticity ( e.g. , consistency regularization under different augmentations) or model stochasticity ( e.g. , difference penalty for predictions of models with different dropout). To take the power of both worlds, we propose a novel χ -model by simultaneously encouraging the invariance to data stochasticity and model stochasticity. Further, the χ -model plays a minimax game between the feature extractor and task-speciﬁc heads to further enhance the invariance to model stochasticity. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: A gap in the literature seems to be a practical completeness threshold for cost optimal planning problems that have actions with 0-cost. This is impractical for most problems since it can be exponentially bigger than the size of the given problem. It should be noted that some approaches try to circumvent the need for a tight completeness threshold, such the ones by Robinson et al. and Leofante et al., which add an over-approximation of the transition relation underlying the planning problem to the encoding. Among them, AirCapRL (Tallamraju et al., 2020) shares similarities with our work. However, it is restricted to coordinating between two cameras in clean landscapes without occlusion. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, they are impractical or neglected to be extended to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, like neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically consume considerable computation resources. In contrast, network pruning is a cheap and effective model compression technique. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. We conduct extensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger image SR networks. SRPN-L and SRPN achieve superior performance gains over recent methods quantitatively and visually.

[ANSWER]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks, such as SRPN-Lite, have achieved promising results with moderate model sizes. However, scaling these networks to larger models is often impractical or ignored. On the other hand, popular model compression techniques, such as neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, can be computationally expensive. In contrast, network pruning is an affordable and effective approach for model compression. However, its application to SR networks is challenging due to the difficulty of pruning filters in residual blocks. To tackle these challenges, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), a method that imposes regularization on the pruned structure to ensure that the locations of pruned filters are consistent across different layers. When the layers are connected by the same residual, we identify the filters with the same indices as unimportant. To transfer the expressive power of unimportant filters to the rest of the network, we use L2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero, leading to minimal performance degradation when these filters are removed. We apply SRP to train efficient SR networks, yielding a lightweight network SRPN-Lite and a deep one called SRPN. We perform comprehensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger SR networks. SRPN-Lite and SRPN deliver superior performance improvements over recent methods, both quantitatively and visually.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, they are impractical or neglected to be extended to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, like neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically consume considerable computation resources. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have obtained promising results with moderate model size. However, they are impractical or neglected to be extended to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, like neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically consume considerable computation resources. In contrast, network pruning is a cheap and effective model compression technique. However, it is hard to be applied to SR networks directly, because ﬁlter pruning for residual blocks is well-known tricky. To address the above issues, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), which imposes regularization on the pruned structure to make sure the locations of pruned ﬁlters are aligned across different layers. Speciﬁcally, for the layers connected by the same residual, we select the ﬁlters of the same indices as unimportant ﬁlters. To transfer the expressive power in the unimportant ﬁlters to the rest of the network, we employ L 2 regularization to drive the weights towards zero so that eventually their absence will cause minimal performance degradation. We apply SRP to train efﬁcient image SR networks, resulting in a lightweight network SRPN-L and a very deep one SRPN. We conduct extensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger image SR networks. SRPN-L and SRPN achieve superior performance gains over recent methods quantitatively and visually.

[ANSWER]: Lightweight image super-resolution (SR) networks have demonstrated considerable promise with relatively compact model sizes. However, they are impractical or often neglected when considering extension to larger networks. At the same time, model compression techniques, such as neural architecture search and knowledge distillation, typically require substantial computational resources. In contrast, network pruning offers an economical and effective model compression technique. Nevertheless, its application to SR networks is challenging, as filter pruning for residual blocks is notoriously complex. To address these challenges, we propose structure-regularized pruning (SRP), a method that imposes regularization on the pruned structure to ensure the alignment of pruned filters across different layers. Specifically, for layers connected by the same residual, we designate filters with identical indices as unimportant. To transfer the expressive power of unimportant filters to the remaining network, L2 regularization is employed to drive the weights towards zero, minimizing performance degradation upon their removal. We apply SRP to train efficient image SR networks, resulting in the development of a lightweight network called SPRN-Lite and a more extensive network, SPRN. We conduct extensive comparisons with both lightweight and larger image SR networks. SPRN-Lite and SPRN achieve superior performance gains over recent methods, both quantitatively and visually.

[ANSWER]: Temporal logic (TL)-guided policy learning is an area that has inspired our work. In this context, TL is often used to specify the ego agent’s desired high-level behavior and to generate rewards. Surveys of recent work on the use of TL in reinforcement learning (RL) can be found in references [17, 18, 19]. A challenge in these methods is the exploration problem. References [20, 21] describe how to learn finite state automata from demonstrations, using them to guide planning with a value iteration network, thereby avoiding exploration. Designing a TL formula manually to yield satisfactory behaviors can be tedious, leading to efforts to make components of the formula learnable from data. For instance, [22] learns linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas from demonstrations. Given the relationship between TL and automata [23], the authors of [24] propose a method for learning reward machines, which are automata-like representations of rewards, from demonstrations. These methods commonly use LTL that operate on propositions (binary variables), requiring either high-level demonstrations (proposition traces) or a mapping from low-level states to propositions. This limitation confines these methods to discrete and finite state and action spaces. In contrast, our method employs signal temporal logic (STL), which works with continuous signals, allowing us to learn from continuous demonstration trajectories that are more readily available in robotic systems. The LogicRiskNet we propose is also learnable from demonstrations.

[ORIGINAL TEXT]: To mitigate the burden of data labeling, we aim at improving data efﬁciency for both classiﬁcation and regression setups in deep learning. However, the current focus is on classiﬁcation problems while rare attention has been paid to deep regression, which usually requires more human effort to labeling. Further, due to the intrinsic difference between categorical and continuous label space, the common intuitions for classiﬁcation, e.g. cluster assumptions or pseudo labeling strategies, cannot be naturally adapted into deep regression. To this end, we ﬁrst delved into the existing data-efﬁcient methods in deep learning and found that they either encourage invariance to data stochasticity ( e.g. , consistency regularization under different augmentations) or model stochasticity ( e.g. , difference penalty for predictions of models with different dropout). To take the power of both worlds, we propose a novel χ -model by simultaneously encouraging the invariance to data stochasticity and model stochasticity. Further, the χ -model plays a minimax game between the feature extractor and task-speciﬁc heads to further enhance the invariance to model stochasticity. Extensive experiments verify the superiority of the χ -model among various tasks, from a single-value prediction task of age estimation to a dense-value prediction task of keypoint localization, a 2D synthetic and a 3D realistic dataset, as well as a multi-category object recognition task.

[ANSWER]: Mahapatra and Rajan (2020) introduced Exact Pareto Optimal (EPO), an MOO optimization method capable of reaching a specified ray in loss space. This solution must exhibit both Pareto optimality and lie at the intersection of the Pareto front and preference vector r. To strike a balance between finding a descent direction and approaching the ray, EPO locates a point within the convex hull of gradient vectors. According to Désidéri (2012), this set encompasses descent directions. EPO subsequently seeks out this point with the most significant angle relative to vector d, which attracts the point towards the preferred ray. Consequently, EPO merges gradient descent and controlled ascent, leading it to attain the exact Pareto optimal solution if one exists or the closest solution if not.

Further, due to the intrinsic difference between categorical and continuous label space, the common intuitions for classiﬁcation, e.g. cluster assumptions or pseudo labeling strategies, cannot be naturally adapted into deep regression. To this end, we ﬁrst delved into the existing data-efﬁcient methods in deep learning and found that they either encourage invariance to data stochasticity ( e.g. , consistency regularization under different augmentations) or model stochasticity ( e.g. , difference penalty for predictions of models with different dropout). Further, the χ -model plays a minimax game between the feature extractor and task-speciﬁc heads to further enhance the invariance to model stochasticity. [ORIGINAL TEXT]: Traditional approaches to predicting the effect of mutation on protein binding can be roughly divided into two classes: biophysical methods and statistical methods. Biophysical methods focus on modeling inter-atomic interactions, e.g. hydrogen bonding, electrostatic forces, etc., with mechanical and statistical energy functions. These methods use their underlying energy function to sample conformations of the mutated protein complex and predict the change in binding free energy upon mutations (Schymkowitz et al., 2005; Park et al., 2016; Alford et al., 2017; Steinbrecher et al., 2017). Statistical methods are based on feature engineering. Descriptors that summarize the geometric, physical, evolutionary, and motif properties of proteinsare used to fit the statistical model that predicts the effect of mutations on binding free energy (Geng et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2020). Traditional methodsgenerally face the trade-off between speed and accuracy due to the time-consuming sampling process. Sophisticated energy functions and feature engineering underlying these methods depend heavily on human knowledge, thus limiting their pace to improve with the fast-growing of available protein structures.

[INSTRUCTION]: Make this paragraph shorter.

[ANSWER]: Approaches to predicting mutation effects on protein binding can be categorized as biophysical methods and statistical methods. Biophysical methods focus on inter-atomic interactions via energy functions. They sample mutated protein complexes using their energy functions to predict binding free energy changes (Schymkowitz et al., 2005; Park et al., 2016; Alford et al., 2017; Steinbrecher et al., 2017). Statistical methods rely on feature engineering, which uses protein descriptors to fit statistical models that predict binding free energy alterations (Geng et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2020). Traditional methods have a speed-accuracy trade-off due to time-consuming sampling processes (Geng et al., 2019b). Their development relies heavily on human knowledge, limiting their pace to advance with the swift expansion of protein structures.

The general decision-making process of an agent in the presence of such model differences is termed model reconciliation (Chakraborti et al. 2017; Zhang et al. 2017).

[ANSWER]: Through our previous research (Chakraborti et al. 2017), we have demonstrated that inconsistencies can be attributed to model differences in the context of generating explanations for human-robot interactions. The reconciliation of such model differences is essential to ensure the human's updated mental model aligns with the robot's behavior, which is critical for the human's understanding and expectation. This process of adjusting mental models in response to observing a robot's behavior in the presence of model differences is referred to as model reconciliation (Chakraborti et al. 2017; Zhang et al. 2017).
